newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt serious on reform, inflows may firm pound - IMF. [CORRECTED 17:56 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Egypt serious on reform, inflows may firm pound - IMF. [CORRECTED 17:56 GMT]

text.p: Egypt is committed to carrying out privatisation and trade reforms and in the past six months has attracted up to $400 million in investment, an International Monetary Fund official said on Wednesday.

Arvind Subramanian, IMF representative in Egypt, said further capital inflows could tend to support the pound (corrects from "could put pressure on the pound") and pose challenges as the government implements its IMF-backed plan.
The deal envisages reforms including privatisation, trade liberalisation, deregulation, greater private sector involvement in the financial system and modernisation of the fiscal system.
Subramanian told Reuters the $400 million in portfolio investment was from April through September. Egypt says it received $50 million in portfolio investment in the year up to June.

"A successful programme might...induce so much capital inflow that in fact the pressure could be in the opposite direction," Subramanian said when asked what could encourage the pound to slip against the dollar.

"I think foreign investor interest in Egypt is on the rise and that might in fact complicate the process (of ensuring a competitive exchange rate). Then of course the government has some very difficult decisions on macro-economic matters.

"Because of course, if capital inflows come in, there is upward pressure on the pound, and therefore a loss in competitiveness," Subramanian said. "This is a problem which has affected many countries."

He said there were no standard solutions but one option would be to "sterilise" the capital inflows. This means the central bank would buy up the foreign exchange and issue securities to mop up the excess liquidity.

The Egyptian government took such a step after foreign exchange liberalisation in the early 1990s. The pound has slipped only by a fraction since then, to 3.40 to the dollar, despite the wide gap between U.S. and Egyptian inflation.
But such a move often "creates a tendency to perpetuate the inflows" and better responses include liberalising trade.

Last week Egypt and the IMF signed a standby credit deal which allows Egypt to withdraw about $200 million a year from the IMF, but Cairo does not intend to draw on the loan because its foreign currency reserves are ample at $18.5 billion.
But the deal could persuade international creditors to scrap Egypt's last tranche of $4 billion official discounted debt.
Egypt has slashed tariffs by up to 25 percent and aims to privatise 91 firms by mid-1998 as part of the reform.
Subramanian said there was political will to privatise in "abundant measure" in Egypt but there were also challenges.
"As you know the privatisation programme this year has got off to a very promising and encouraging start," he said. "There are going to be challenges in the next phase of privatisation."
He said these included finding anchor investors and privatising firms which needed infusions such as of technology.
Subramanian said an "important clue to the government's intention in the future" was that Egypt was "embracing globalisation and integrating itself with international markets.

"What this means is that it basically entails a precommitment to play by the standards of international markets. If there are any slip-ups in policy then markets can be very brutal in disciplining errant government behaviour. It (Egypt) is willing to keep up the pace of implementation of reforms."
He said the IMF's first review will be based on end of December performance but the review would be months later.
